items.item: Open addressing's entire reason for existing is to avoid chaining's one named cost (a pointer per entry) by storing every entry directly in the table itself, at the cost of a probe sequence when two keys compete for a slot.

at.step: Chaining pays a pointer per entry. Open addressing gives that up — every entry lives in the table itself.

items.item: Linear probing's mechanism is the simplest possible probe step (always +1), and that same simplicity is exactly what causes primary clustering: a collision with a run almost always extends it, and longer runs catch more future collisions.

at.step: Linear probing's own collisions make its runs longer, and longer runs catch even more of the next collisions.

items.item: Quadratic probing and double hashing are two different, real fixes for primary clustering, with two different trade-offs — quadratic probing needs a prime table size and α < 0.5 for its own guarantee and still suffers secondary clustering; double hashing avoids both at the cost of computing a second hash function per probe.

at.step: Two real fixes: quadratic probing scatters instead of extending a run; double hashing diverges immediately.

items.item: The syllabus names Knuth's expected-probe analysis specifically; this topic cites Knuth's own paper (total displacement d, average successful-search cost 1 + d/n) for that attribution, kept honestly distinct from the MIT lecture's separate uniform-hashing-assumption bound (1/(1-α)) that examples.py actually measures against — the two are related but not the same derivation.

Deleting an entry from an open-addressed table can't simply empty its slot, because a later probe sequence passing through would stop at the empty slot and miss entries placed beyond it — this is the one correctness subtlety both tombstones and backward-shift (cluster-rehash) deletion exist to solve, each at a different cost.

at.step: A tombstone keeps a slot occupied forever; rehashing the cluster costs a scan now instead.

items.item: A tombstone and cluster-rehash deletion are not equivalent in cost: a tombstone keeps its slot occupied forever, shrinking the table's effective capacity until a rehash reclaims it; cluster-rehash pays a bounded extra scan immediately but frees the slot right away.

at.step: A tombstone keeps a slot occupied forever; rehashing the cluster costs a scan now instead.

items.item: The table-is-full question (what happens when no empty slot exists, or when to resize under memory pressure) is explicitly this chapter's own topic 20, not built here.

Robin Hood hashing and cuckoo hashing are more elaborate probe-sequence designs that trade extra bookkeeping for tighter worst-case guarantees than plain linear probing, double hashing, or quadratic probing offer — named with no mechanism, since the syllabus skips both for this chapter.

at.out: Syllabus names Robin Hood hashing and cuckoo hashing nowhere in this chapter's run — both are skipped, named only in post-notes' frontier section with no mechanism.

items.item: Double hashing's own correctness requirement (h2(k) relatively prime to m) is satisfiable by a simple, standard construction: pick a prime table size, so every nonzero step is automatically coprime to it — the same construction examples.py uses.

at.step: Two real fixes: quadratic probing scatters instead of extending a run; double hashing diverges immediately.

items.item: Linear probing's average-probe measurement and Knuth's own displacement-based result are related by the same underlying mechanism (how far, on average, keys land from their hash address) but are not interchangeable citations — this topic's examples.py measures the uniform-hashing-assumption quantity, not Knuth's own combinatorial displacement distribution.
